idiom_name: Option<T> with Some/None, the ? operator and match
implementation_notes: Rust has no null references: absence is the core enum Option<T> { None, Some(T) }, and the two cases are the only shape the value has - pattern matching, the combinators (map/and_then/filter/unwrap_or/or_else/zip) and the ? operator (which early-returns None from a function returning Option) are the routes to the payload. The library documents the uses directly (initial values, partial functions, simple errors, optional fields, nullable pointers). Representation is usually free: for Box<T>, references, NonZero* and fn pointers the compiler guarantees that Option<T> has the same size, alignment and ABI as T (the null-pointer optimization). Option is for absence without a reason; Result<T, E> with ok_or/ok_or_else is the type for failures. The classic hand-written Maybe enum is replaced by the core type; a custom two-case enum is justified only when the absence must carry a meaning that Option cannot (which is normally Result's job).
pitfalls: unwrap()/expect() panic on None - the Rust form of the null dereference; reserve them for tests and invariants the type cannot express and use ?/unwrap_or_else in production paths.
Option cannot carry a reason: using None for 'invalid' as well as 'absent' loses the diagnosis Result preserves - convert with ok_or_else at that boundary.
The null-pointer optimization is guaranteed only for the listed types (Box, references, NonZero, fn); Option<u32> is larger than u32, which matters in hot loops and large arrays.
&Option<T> as a parameter is an anti-idiom: accept Option<&T> or a borrowed value (as_deref) so callers are not tied to the wrapper's shape.
